doc.title: Elvin Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: What he looks for in musicians for his band
summary: He wants maturity, command of the instrument, and sincerity, judging by hearing them play.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: So what do you look for, what are the criteria; what are the qualities in a musician you look for, to bring them into the Elvin Jones Ensemble? What are the things you’re looking for in a musician?

Well, first they have to be, they have to be, a certain amount of maturity has to be there within whoever the guy is. They understand what the command of the instrument is all about. A lot of people want jobs but they’re not prepared. You know, they haven’t studied enough, they haven’t….they don’t know the scales. And if you don’t know the scales then you’re not ready to play with anybody. That’s important that they know, that they know about to do and they’ve prepared themselves for that. Same if you’ve made an audition for the Philharmonic. What’s the difference?

There is the issue of technical facility but what about a particular artistic vision? Particularly in jazz, you have to be able to improvise so you have to make a statement as well as being able to play somebody else’s music. So, how do you play…how do you judge somebody’s solo or improvisational ability?

Well if you hear ‘em play that should tell you. That gives you all the information you need if they can come in and be a part of that orchestra. Not even for any reward or anything like that. “Oh you’re going to have the job for four or six months” or “Oh we’re

going into the studio and record.” It’s not that. You have to know how to play. You have to know, to be… As I said, that’s part of being mature and being grown. You have to be adult with respects, so that you’re not what the people used to call a “shuck-in”. (Laughs) So you’re not shucking. When a cat is straight, he doesn’t have any problems. Usually people are very sincere about that.

I bring this up, and I’m glad that you qualify it, because there are many, many brilliant musicians but, as far as their sense of responsibility, or, like you say, the maturity, sure they’re technical wizards, they’re musical geniuses, but personally, they may be not able to make that type of commitment you talk about…
…that’s necessary to bring the group together. That must be something that you’re observing before they get in the group. I’m sure you’re observing, checking, and monitoring that.

I try to be sure that person is qualified before. I say, “This is not a jam session. We’re serious.” You have to be prepared for that. Normally I don’t have any problems because anytime someone comes to me they are more than ready. I’ve been lucky that way.
